blogs.title: Umar Khalid Case: UAPA and the Question of Constitutional Rights
blogs.excerpt: An in-depth analysis of the Umar Khalid case, examining the intersection of UAPA provisions, fundamental rights, and the prolonged detention of activists arrested during the Delhi riots.
blogs.content:
Background

On 14th September 2020, Umar Khalid, former PhD scholar in JNU and political activist, along with other activists and protestors, were arrested by Delhi Police Special Cell in connection to Delhi North-East Riots. They were arrested under the suspicion of inciting Delhi riots, which led to 54 recorded deaths and various injuries. All the protestors against CAA-NRC were charged with various offences including various provisions under IPC and UAPA including Section 16 which states that punishment for terrorism shall be death penalty. Provisions under IPC, including rioting (Sections 147, 148), murder (Section 302), unlawful assembly (Section 149), sedition (Section 124A), and promoting enmity between groups (Section 153A).

Delhi Police refers to him as the 'key conspirator' of the riots, who, along with others, allegedly planned and orchestrated the riots during protests that turned violent. He is charged for making 'provocative speech' and bringing as well as organising and inducing feelings of dissent in the common masses. Khalid denies all the said charges and called them politically motivated.

Historical Background of UAPA

The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), enacted in 1967, aims to effectively prevent unlawful actions by individuals or groups that threaten India's sovereignty and integrity. In the 1960s, rising communalism, regionalism, and threats to national unity led the government to empower Parliament with constitutional amendments, permitting reasonable restrictions on freedoms of speech, assembly, and association. The UAPA was enacted to implement these powers, targeting secessionist, terrorist, and anti-national activities. Its objectives include preventing such unlawful activities, prosecuting terrorist acts, and empowering the government to designate individuals and organizations as terrorists. The Act has been amended multiple times to address evolving security challenges, including the 2019 amendment allowing designation of individual terrorists, reflecting India's response to modern threats to national security.

Key Contentions

1. Khalid is termed a 'key conspirator' behind the incitement of violence which broke out in Delhi. There is a clear nexus between Anti CAA-NRC protest and riots which broke out in the light of it.

2. UAPA is a restrictive law and the court can deny bail if there seems a prima facie valid case. The 'notwithstanding' clause in both evidence law and criminal procedural law supports the same argument.

3. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta said that the accused must be kept in jail until they either get acquitted or convicted.

Question of Law v. Saga of Defence Counsel

Senior advocate Kapil Sibal is representing Umar Khalid in his bail matter for Delhi riots and UAPA proceedings. The senior counsel over the span of 5 years has conducted various press conferences and opted for various mechanisms such as media debates and interviews to keep Umar Khalid's voice.

1. Incarceration for over 5 years without bail is not usual, but it is the reality of few protestors. Mr. Sibal's main arguments on Umar's issue is that there is a sheer violation of Fundamental Rights under Article 21 of the Indian Constitution which guarantees right to life and liberty; it has been denied by continuous incarceration. Khalid has been behind the bars for over 5 years now.

2. The major nexus upon which the entire case of prosecution stands is the rational nexus of connection between violence and CAA-NRC protest. The prosecution has failed to establish a connection between Delhi riots and CAA-NRC protest as the cause of violence which lead to death and injury of the many. There is no question mark upon the existence of these two events, but establishing the connection between the two needs to be proven.

3. India is the largest democracy in the world, one of the major pillars for safeguarding and protection of democracy is dissent. Mr. Sibal highlights that Right to protest is a fundamental right protected under Article 19 that is Right to speech and expression, mere dissent towards a policy or law shall not tantamount to UAPA charges.

4. The bail and chargesheet doctrine which is being followed in cases of UAPA is different from the one which is commonly used under CrPc, now BNSS. The status of chargesheet under criminal jurisprudence as a general rule is that, it is merely a point of view of the investigating agency and should not be very strictly scrutinised for grant of bail. Whereas under Section 43D(5), UAPA gives chargesheet uttermost importance, the existence of whether case prima facie exists or not is based completely on chargesheet, if proven so the bail shall be denied.

However, Mr. Sibal argues that the chargesheet can not be treated as more than just a point of view of investigating authorities, not a conclusive proof. Citing judicial precedents in UAPA cases, Sibal lamented that 'the Supreme Court violates its own decisions'. The judicial decisions cited by him included – Athar Parwez v. Union of India (accused spent 2 years 4 months in jail; got bail); Shoma Kantil Sen v. State (accused spent 6 year in jail; got bail); Jahir Haq v. State of Rajasthan (accused spent 8 years in jail; got bail) and Union of India v K.A Najeeb (accused spent 5 years in jail, got bail). It was mentioned that in some of these cases, even charges had been framed, which is not the case with Khalid.

5. Mr. Sibal also presents his concern over the fact that prosecution has not presented the alleged videos and around 700 witnesses, if the same is presented there shall be some clarity given and the court can reach a conclusion of the real faces behind the violence which broke. The admissibility of electronic evidence is subjected to lack of provisions in Indian Evidence Act, which does not accommodate videographic evidence. Since the arrest was made in 2020 so the provisions of IEA shall prevail not but provisions of BSA shall, by the virtue of Section 160(Saving clause), which states that it does not have retrospective effect and any case before the date of enforcement of Bhartiya Sakshya Adhiniyam shall be dealt in the light of IEA.

Conclusion

Bail is the rule, jail is the expectation is the commonly accepted doctrine of criminal jurisprudence, anyhow in the special laws under defined statute has different rules to be followed. While the contention of the defences holds a very strong space but they are not administered and accepted by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi. The country clearly seems to be divided into two separate groups, one which supports the undefined and what seems like an infinite incarceration of alleged anti nationals and key conspirators of Delhi North-East Riots; while the other group's lobby echo with the reasoning of one's fundamental rights and human rights.

blogs.title: Understanding the Consumer Protection Act 2019: Your Rights and Remedies
blogs.excerpt: A comprehensive guide to the Consumer Protection Act 2019, exploring the rights of consumers, the establishment of consumer disputes redressal commissions, and how to file effective complaints.
blogs.content:
The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 represents a significant milestone in safeguarding consumer rights in India. This legislation replaced the Consumer Protection Act of 1986 and introduced several progressive provisions to address the changing dynamics of consumer markets in the digital age.

Key Features of the Act

The Act establishes a three-tier consumer disputes redressal system: District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, and National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission. Each tier has defined pecuniary jurisdiction to handle consumer complaints.

Consumer Rights

Under this Act, consumers are entitled to six fundamental rights: the right to safety, the right to be informed, the right to choose, the right to be heard, the right to seek redressal, and the right to consumer education. These rights form the foundation of consumer protection in India.

E-Commerce and Product Liability

The 2019 Act specifically addresses e-commerce transactions and introduces product liability provisions. E-commerce platforms now have defined responsibilities, and manufacturers, service providers, and sellers can be held liable for defective products or deficient services.

Unfair Trade Practices

The Act provides protection against unfair trade practices, including false or misleading advertisements, deceptive pricing, and pyramid schemes. The Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) has been established to investigate and take suo moto action against violations.

Filing a Consumer Complaint

Consumers can file complaints within two years from the date of cause of action. The complaint must include details of the defect or deficiency, relevant documents, and the relief sought. The process has been simplified with provisions for online filing and video conferencing for hearings.

Remedies Available

Consumer forums can order various remedies including removal of defects, replacement of goods, refund of price, compensation for loss or injury, and costs of litigation. Punitive damages can also be awarded in cases of gross negligence or malicious conduct.

Conclusion

The Consumer Protection Act 2019 empowers consumers with robust mechanisms to protect their rights and seek effective redressal. Understanding these provisions helps consumers make informed decisions and take appropriate action when faced with unfair practices or deficient services.

blogs.title: Article 32: The Heart and Soul of the Constitution
blogs.excerpt: Exploring Article 32 of the Indian Constitution, which Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called the most important article, and its role as the guardian of fundamental rights through constitutional remedies.
blogs.content:
Article 32 of the Indian Constitution, rightly described by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar as 'the heart and soul of the Constitution,' guarantees the right to constitutional remedies for the enforcement of fundamental rights. This article empowers citizens to approach the Supreme Court directly when their fundamental rights are violated.

The Right to Constitutional Remedies

Article 32 ensures that fundamental rights are not mere declarations but are enforceable rights. Without this article, the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part III of the Constitution would be meaningless promises. The Supreme Court is constitutionally bound to protect these rights and cannot refuse to exercise its jurisdiction under this article.

Writ Jurisdiction

Under Article 32, the Supreme Court can issue five types of writs: Habeas Corpus (for personal liberty), Mandamus (to compel performance of public duty), Prohibition (to prevent excess of jurisdiction), Certiorari (for quashing orders), and Quo Warranto (to question authority). These writs serve as powerful tools for protecting fundamental rights.

Public Interest Litigation (PIL)

The Supreme Court has liberalized the concept of locus standi under Article 32, allowing any public-spirited person to approach the court on behalf of those whose rights have been violated but who cannot approach the court themselves due to poverty, ignorance, or social disability. This innovation has made justice more accessible to marginalized sections of society.

Limitations and Exceptions

While Article 32 is a fundamental right, it can be suspended during a national emergency under Article 359. However, writs for the enforcement of Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during an emergency. The court also exercises judicial restraint and may refuse to entertain frivolous petitions.

Recent Developments

In recent years, the Supreme Court has used its Article 32 jurisdiction to address pressing social issues including environmental protection, women's rights, education, healthcare, and prison reforms. The court has issued numerous directions to ensure effective implementation of fundamental rights.

Article 32 vs Article 226

While High Courts also have writ jurisdiction under Article 226, Article 32 differs in that it is itself a fundamental right, and the Supreme Court cannot refuse to exercise this power. High Courts, however, have discretion in exercising their writ jurisdiction.

Conclusion

Article 32 stands as a testimony to the founding fathers' commitment to making India a just society. It transforms the Supreme Court into the guardian of fundamental rights and ensures that constitutional guarantees are not hollow promises but living realities for every citizen of India.

blogs.title: Corporate Compliance in 2024: Navigating the New Legal Landscape
blogs.excerpt: An essential guide for businesses on compliance requirements under the Companies Act 2013, including recent amendments, ESG obligations, and best practices for corporate governance.
blogs.content:
Corporate compliance has become increasingly complex in India, with multiple regulatory bodies overseeing different aspects of business operations. The Companies Act 2013, along with numerous amendments and rules, forms the backbone of corporate law in India.

Corporate Governance Framework

The Companies Act 2013 introduced significant changes to corporate governance norms, including mandatory provisions for independent directors, audit committees, and board evaluation. Listed companies must comply with additional requirements under SEBI regulations, including mandatory disclosures and corporate governance reports.

Statutory Compliance Requirements

Companies must comply with various statutory requirements including annual general meetings, board meetings, maintenance of statutory registers, filing of annual returns and financial statements with the Registrar of Companies, and payment of annual fees. Non-compliance can result in penalties and prosecution of officers in default.

Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG)

ESG compliance has gained prominence with the introduction of Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) for top 1000 listed companies. Companies must now disclose their performance on environmental and social parameters, making sustainability a core business consideration.

Data Protection and Privacy

With the enactment of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023, companies handling personal data must comply with new obligations regarding data collection, processing, and storage. This includes obtaining consent, ensuring data security, and respecting data principal rights.

Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR)

Companies meeting specified thresholds must spend at least 2% of their average net profits on CSR activities. The law mandates formation of CSR committees, preparation of CSR policies, and detailed reporting of CSR spending. Unspent amounts must be transferred to specified funds.

Related Party Transactions

The Act has stringent provisions regarding related party transactions to prevent conflict of interest and ensure fairness. Companies must obtain necessary approvals and make required disclosures for related party transactions exceeding specified thresholds.

Insider Trading Regulations

SEBI's insider trading regulations prohibit directors, officers, and connected persons from trading in securities based on unpublished price-sensitive information. Companies must establish robust systems to prevent insider trading and ensure compliance with disclosure requirements.

Risk Management

Top companies are required to constitute risk management committees and implement comprehensive risk management frameworks. This includes identifying, assessing, and mitigating various risks including financial, operational, and reputational risks.

Whistleblower Mechanism

Companies must establish vigil mechanisms for directors and employees to report genuine concerns about unethical behavior, fraud, or violation of company's code of conduct. The mechanism must ensure adequate safeguards against victimization.

Conclusion

Corporate compliance is no longer a mere checklist exercise but requires a holistic approach integrating legal, ethical, and governance considerations. Companies must invest in robust compliance systems, regular training, and internal audits to navigate the evolving regulatory landscape successfully.
